newsitem.title: USA: Philly oversight board sees 'major risks' in plan.
newsitem.headline: Philly oversight board sees 'major risks' in plan.

text.p: Philadelphia's oversight board Wednesday said it sees "major risks" that $321 million of revenues the city is counting on over the next five years will never materialize.

"The city's reliance upon these highly questionable revenue generating sources and expense reductions raises concerns as to whether the city can meet its balanced budget projections laid out in the five-year plan," Joseph Vignola, executive director of the Pennsylvania Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority, said in a statement.
Vignola said, however, that Mayor Ed Rendell has time to address the problems, which center on what Vignola called "non-existent tax revenues and unspecified expenditure reductions."
Despite its concerns, PICA approved the five-year fiscal plan on Tuesday.
Vignola said the biggest problem area is an outstanding legal challenge to the city's collection of the personal property tax, which accounts for $162 million of the revenue concern.

"The city's imposition of a substitute tax may be challenged, possibly resulting in the termination of the tax revenue and the city's being held liable for the refund of such taxes paid since 1993," PICA said.

The city is also counting on $89 million of revenues, beginning in fiscal 2000, from riverboat gambling. The state Legislature, which must approve that proposal, has consistently balked at the idea. PICA called the plan's inclusion of gambling revenues "highly speculative."
Finally, PICA criticized Rendell's reliance on $70 million of unidentified "future target spending reductions" in each of the last four years of the plan.
